newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends higher in lackluster trade.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends higher in lackluster trade.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended higher Tuesday in lackluster trade that was marked by little fundamental news, industry sources said.

Western futures and physical power trade was overshadowed Tuesday for skyrocketing prices in the U.S. Midwest and the northeast due to warm, humid weather and some transmission constraints, the sources said.
"The lack of cash trade (in the U.S. West) has kind of hit us in terms of activity," said one Houston-based electricity futures trader.
July Palo Verde (PV) ended up 64 cents at $33.35 following exchanges in a range of $32.15-33.50, while August PV ended up 95 cents at $34.85 after trades at $33.90-34.90 per megawatt hour (MWh).

July California Oregon Border (COB) ended up 52 cents at $20.86 after exchanges in a range of $20.10-20.40, while August settled up 71 cents at 23.90 per MWh after exchanges in a range of $23.20-24.20 per MWh.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 1,063 PV and 1,071 COB contracts traded.
The July PV and COB contracts expire Wednesday.

Sources said July COB may have found support late in the day from rumors a restart of the 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state might be pushed back beyond expectations of later this week.
Restart of the plant still requires Nuclear Regulatory Commission approval, but Bonneville Power Administration has said it hopes the unit will resume output late next week.
In the Pacific Southwest, temperatures were expected to be between zero and five degrees Fahrenheit below normal through mid-week, rising to near normal to above normal by the end of the month.
Northwest temperatures were forecast at four to eight degrees below normal through mid-week, rising to above normal by next week.

In generation news, the 750 megawatt (MW) unit 5 at the Four Corners coal-fired power plant in New Mexico was near 100 percent capacity after starting to ramp up on Monday. The unit had tripped off-line last Wednesday due to a tube rupture.

Separately, the Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) board is expected to approve a plan later this week, which calls for the Pacific Intertie transmission system to be derated from July 1-30 to 6,300 megawatt (MW) from the current limit of 7,200 MW.
